extracted.intended_audience: agency staff, regulatory attorneys, and stakeholders tracking Congressional Review Act (CRA) disapprovals and resulting Federal Register/CFR corrections
extracted.subtask_description: A consolidated search-results listing Federal Register documents and excerpts concerning actions taken under the Congressional Review Act (disapprovals, revocations, exemptions, procedural notes, and corrections). Useful for finding how agencies implement CRA effects (removal from the CFR, effective dates, OMB determinations, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of CRA disapproval (nullification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Congressional Review Act, Congress passed, and the President signed, a joint resolution disapproving [a] final rule; under the joint resolution and by operation of the CRA, the [disapproved] rule has no legal force or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple excerpts state the same principle (e.g., "Under the joint resolution and by operation of the CRA, the 2024 Rule has no legal force or effect." and "Under the joint resolution and by operation of the CRA, this final rule has no legal force or effect."). Agencies implementing a disapproval should treat the disapproved final rule as nullified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency duty to remove disapproved rule from the CFR / restore prior text
rubrics_metrics.description: When a final rule is disapproved under the CRA, agencies remove that final rule from the Code of Federal Regulations and, where applicable, revert the relevant CFR text to the text that was in effect immediately prior to the effective date of the disapproved rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts: "The Department ... hereby remove this final rule from the Code of Federal Regulations and revert the relevant text of the CFR back to the text that was in effect immediately prior to the effective date of this final rule." and "DOE has a nondiscretionary duty to remove the associated provisions from the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR)." Agencies often publish final rules in the Federal Register formalizing the withdrawal and conforming amendments to the CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial nature / notice-and-comment exemption for CRA withdrawals
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawing a final rule that has been disapproved under the CRA can be treated as ministerial, making notice-and-comment (under APA 5 U.S.C. 553) unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts: "This action is exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking because it is ministerial in nature." and "To the extent that 5 U.S.C. 553 applies to this action, DOE finds that notice and comment is unnecessary because DOE is withdrawing a final rule that has been disapproved under the Congressional Review Act." Agencies should explain why the withdrawal is ministerial when declining notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB determination of 'major rule' status
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the CRA, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) makes a determination as to whether a final rule constitutes a 'major' rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts: "For purposes of the Congressional Review Act, the OMB makes a determination as to whether a final rule constitutes a 'major' rule." and "The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs determined this rule does not meet the criteria for a 'major rule' under 5 U.S.C. 804(2)." Agencies routinely state OMB's determination in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of 'major rule' designation — 60-day delay
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule is deemed a 'major rule' by OMB, the CRA generally provides that the rule may not take effect until at least 60 days following its publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts: "If a rule is deemed a 'major rule' by OMB, the Congressional Review Act generally provides that the rule may not take effect until at least 60 days following its publication." and agencies correct effective dates when they inadvertently listed an earlier effective date that violated the CRA-required delay. Agencies must therefore check and, if necessary, correct effective dates to comply with the CRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRA submission requirement before rule takes effect
rubrics_metrics.description: As required by the Congressional Review Act (5 U.S.C. 801-808), agencies must submit a copy of an interim or final rule to Congress (and to OMB/Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs) before the rule takes effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpt: "As required by the Congressional Review Act (5 U.S.C. 801-808) before an interim or final rule takes effect, DoD will submit a copy of..." Agencies commonly state they will submit or have submitted the rule as required by the CRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRA exemptions / categories of nonapplicability (5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C) and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rules or actions are exempt from the Congressional Review Act pursuant to statutory exemptions (e.g., 5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C)), and agencies may state when a particular rule falls within an exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpt: "This rule is exempt from the Congressional Review Act, pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C)." Agencies should cite the statutory exemption and explain why it applies when asserting an exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRA covers many agency actions including guidance that meet the statutory 'rule' definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents such as Regulatory Guides (RGs) and Interim Staff Guidance (ISG) can be considered 'rules' as defined in the CRA (5 U.S.C. 801-808), and thus may be subject to CRA procedures even if OMB does not find them 'major.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts: "This RG is a rule as defined in the Congressional Review Act (5 U.S.C. 801-808)." and "This ISG is a rule as defined in the Congressional Review Act (5 U.S.C. 801-808)." Agencies should state CRA applicability for guidance-like documents and note OMB's major/non-major finding where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must correct preamble/regulatory text to ensure CRA compliance (effective dates/citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a final rule's preamble or regulatory text incorrectly lists an effective date or other compliance detail that conflicts with CRA requirements, agencies must publish corrections (e.g., correct effective date to reflect required 60-day delay; correct citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpt: "The effective date of that final rule was listed in the preamble as the date of publication ... when it should have had the required 60-day delay to comply with the Congressional Review Act. The effective date should have been October 21, 2024." Agencies commonly issue an 'Announcement and Correction' or correction rule to fix such errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondiscretionary nature of removing CRA-disapproved provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a final rule has been disapproved under the CRA and thus has no force or effect, the agency's obligation to remove the disapproved provisions from the CFR is nondiscretionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpt: "Because the October 9, 2024 final rule has no force or effect, DOE has a nondiscretionary duty to remove the associated provisions from the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), and through this final rule, DOE is taking the necessary action to effect such rescission." Agencies often describe the action as ministerial but nondiscretionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancillary procedural notes commonly paired with CRA actions (judicial review, executive orders, info collections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Register notices concerning CRA actions routinely include other regulatory procedural statements (e.g., judicial review filing deadlines under underlying statutes, statements under Executive Orders such as E.O. 12866, Paperwork Reduction Act findings, NMFA/Unfunded Mandates determinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in excerpts: "Under CAA section 307(b)(1), any petition for review of this final rule must be filed ... by July 18, 2025." and various notices state OMB/Executive Order reviews or PRA conclusions. These are not CRA requirements themselves but are standard preamble elements agencies include alongside CRA-related actions.
